html:
The siege of Bursa was a long blockade that ended on 6 April 1326, when the Byzantine city of Prusa, today's Bursa in northwest Turkey, surrendered to the Ottomans. It was the first large city they took, and it became their first real capital.

Osman, founder of the Ottoman state, had beaten a Byzantine army at Bapheus in 1302 and controlled the countryside of Bithynia. But his followers were horsemen with no siege engines and could not storm walls. So they built forts near Prusa and cut it off from its farms and from the sea. The blockade went on for years. Sources say six to nine. The Byzantine Empire was busy with a civil war and sent no relief. In the end hunger made the governor give up. Osman died about this time, and it was his son Orhan who took over the city.

Orhan made Bursa his capital, struck coins there and buried his father in it. A band of frontier raiders had become a state with a city, a market and a court. Nicaea fell in 1331 and Nicomedia in 1337, and in the 1350s the Ottomans crossed into Europe.
